claim: Magnetotactic cocci with two flagella bundles on one pole swim faster than 500 µm·s−1 along a double helical path.
source: We show that magnetotactic cocci with two flagella bundles on one pole swim faster than 500 µm·s−1 along a double helical path, making them one of the fastest natural microswimmers.
evidence: Supported by experimental tracking data showing instantaneous traveling speeds between 100 µm s−1 and 500 µm s−1 (Figure 1D) and double helical path observations.

claim: Magnetotactic cocci are one of the fastest natural microswimmers.
source: We show that magnetotactic cocci with two flagella bundles on one pole swim faster than 500 µm·s−1 along a double helical path, making them one of the fastest natural microswimmers.
evidence: Based on comparison with previously reported swimming speeds of other bacteria (several 10 µm s−1) and measured speeds over 500 µm·s−1.

claim: MC-1 cells reorient in less than 5 ms.
source: We additionally reveal that the cells reorient in less than 5 ms, an order of magnitude faster than reported so far for any other bacteria.
evidence: Supported by high-speed tracking data showing reorientation events lasting 2.5-5 ms.

claim: MC-1 reorientation is an order of magnitude faster than reported for any other bacteria.
source: We additionally reveal that the cells reorient in less than 5 ms, an order of magnitude faster than reported so far for any other bacteria.
evidence: Based on comparison with previously reported reorientation times of 50-100 ms for other bacteria (Son et al., 2013; Berg and Brown, 1972).

claim: A mode where a pushing and a pulling bundle cooperate is the only possibility to enable both helical tracks and fast reorientations in MC-1.
source: Using hydrodynamic modeling, we demonstrate that a mode where a pushing and a pulling bundle cooperate is the only possibility to enable both helical tracks and fast reorientations.
evidence: Demonstrated through Stokesian dynamics simulations testing multiple flagella configurations, where only CCW and CW rotation produced matching experimental observations.

claim: The advantage of sheathed flagella bundles is the high rigidity, making high swimming speeds possible.
source: The advantage of sheathed flagella bundles is the high rigidity, making high swimming speeds possible.
evidence: Supported by simulation requirements of high isotropic bending and twisting rigidities (7 pN μm2) to achieve stable high swimming velocities.

claim: Escherichia coli is peritrichous with several flagella all over the body surface.
source: Well-studied examples of swimming microorganisms include the peritrichous (several flagella all over the body surface) Escherichia coli with an occasionally distorted hydrodynamic flagella bundling (Turner et al., 2000)
evidence: Cited from established literature on bacterial flagellar arrangements.

claim: Vibrio alginolyticus is monotrichous with one polar flagellum.
source: the monotrichous (one polar flagellum) Vibrio alginolyticus, which are pushed or pulled by a flagellum and exploit a mechanical buckling instability to change direction (Xie et al., 2011; Son et al., 2013)
evidence: Cited from established literature on bacterial flagellar arrangements.

claim: Vibrio alginolyticus exploits a mechanical buckling instability to change direction.
source: the monotrichous (one polar flagellum) Vibrio alginolyticus, which are pushed or pulled by a flagellum and exploit a mechanical buckling instability to change direction (Xie et al., 2011; Son et al., 2013)
evidence: Cited from previous research on V. alginolyticus motility mechanisms.

claim: Swimming speeds of previously studied cells are in the range of several 10 µm s−1.
source: The swimming speeds of so far studied cells are in the range of several 10 µm s−1 and their reorientation events occur on the time scale of 50–100 ms (Son et al., 2013; Berg and Brown, 1972).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on bacterial swimming speeds.

claim: Reorientation events in previously studied bacteria occur on the time scale of 50–100 ms.
source: The swimming speeds of so far studied cells are in the range of several 10 µm s−1 and their reorientation events occur on the time scale of 50–100 ms (Son et al., 2013; Berg and Brown, 1972).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on bacterial reorientation dynamics.

claim: Magnetococcus marinus (MC-1) is a magnetotactic, spherical bacterium that is capable of swimming extremely fast.
source: Magnetococcus marinus (MC-1) is a magnetotactic, spherical bacterium that is capable of swimming extremely fast (Zhang et al., 2014; Fenchel and Thar, 2004; Bazylinski et al., 2013; Garcia-Pichel, 1989).
evidence: Cited from previous literature on MC-1 characteristics.

claim: MC-1 and the closely related strain MO-1 are equipped with two bundles of flagella on one hemisphere (bilophotrichous cells).
source: MC-1 as well as the closely related strain MO-1 (Ruan et al., 2012) are equipped with two bundles of flagella on one hemisphere (bilophotrichous cells).
evidence: Cited from previous literature and confirmed by TEM imaging in this study.

claim: MC-1 features a magnetosome chain, which imparts the cell with a magnetic moment.
source: The bacterium also features a magnetosome chain, which imparts the cell with a magnetic moment ('magnetotactic' cell).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of magnetotactic bacteria and confirmed by experimental observations.

claim: MC-1 was previously assumed to swim with the cell body in front of both flagella bundles, which synchronously push the cell forward.
source: They are assumed to swim with the cell body in front of both flagella bundles, which synchronously push the cell forward (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous literature as a prior assumption that this study challenges.

claim: The previous model of MC-1 swimming predicts helical motion in the presence of a strong magnetic field.
source: This assumption leads to helical motion in the presence of a strong magnetic field, which exerts a torque on the cell's magnetic moment, as seen in hydrodynamic simulations (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous hydrodynamic simulations.

claim: The previous model of MC-1 swimming predicts rather straight trajectories in the absence of a magnetic field.
source: In the absence of a magnetic field, this model predicts rather straight trajectories.
evidence: Logical inference from the previous model's assumptions about synchronized pushing flagella.

claim: The authors' observations disagree with the previous model of MC-1 swimming.
source: Our observations disagree with the above-mentioned model, indicating that an understanding of the physics of their swimming is still missing
evidence: Based on experimental observations of double helical paths in the absence of magnetic fields, contradicting predictions of straight trajectories.

claim: MC-1 cells reach speeds of over 500 µm s−1.
source: Here, we confirm that MC-1 cells reach speeds of over 500 µm s−1 (Figure 1D)
evidence: Confirmed by experimental tracking data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: MC-1 cells have an extremely fast reorientation ability (less than 5 ms).
source: In addition, we observed that this rapid movement is complemented by an extremely fast reorientation ability (less than 5 ms).
evidence: Measured from high-speed tracking data showing reorientation events lasting 2.5-5 ms.

claim: Only a cooperative movement where one flagella bundle pushes while the other pulls the cell explains MC-1's motility characteristics.
source: We connect the flagella bundle architecture and the swimming mechanism by hydrodynamic simulations and show that only a striking cooperative movement where one flagella bundle pushes while the other pulls the cell explains these motility characteristics.
evidence: Demonstrated through systematic testing of different flagellar rotation scenarios in Stokesian dynamics simulations.

claim: MC-1 cells traveled on helical paths with a pitch of 5.3 µm ± 1.3 µm in the absence of magnetic torques.
source: Our first set of observations revealed that the cells traveled on helical paths (with a pitch of 5.3 µm ± 1.3 µm, a diameter of 1.7 µm ± 0.2 µm, and a period of 46 ms ± 32 ms, n = 65, errors are standard deviations) in the absence of magnetic torques
evidence: Measured from 3D tracking data with automated track analysis algorithm.

claim: MC-1 cells traveled on helical paths with a diameter of 1.7 µm ± 0.2 µm in the absence of magnetic torques.
source: Our first set of observations revealed that the cells traveled on helical paths (with a pitch of 5.3 µm ± 1.3 µm, a diameter of 1.7 µm ± 0.2 µm, and a period of 46 ms ± 32 ms, n = 65, errors are standard deviations) in the absence of magnetic torques
evidence: Measured from 3D tracking data with automated track analysis algorithm.

claim: MC-1 cells traveled on helical paths with a period of 46 ms ± 32 ms in the absence of magnetic torques.
source: Our first set of observations revealed that the cells traveled on helical paths (with a pitch of 5.3 µm ± 1.3 µm, a diameter of 1.7 µm ± 0.2 µm, and a period of 46 ms ± 32 ms, n = 65, errors are standard deviations) in the absence of magnetic torques
evidence: Measured from 3D tracking data with automated track analysis algorithm.

claim: Abrupt changes of the direction of the helical axis occur within 2.5 ms to 5 ms in MC-1.
source: In addition, abrupt changes of the direction of the helical axis were observed (e.g. around 90° in Figure 1—figure supplement 3). These directional changes occur within 2.5 ms to 5 ms, at least one order of magnitude faster than any previously analyzed reorientation events (Son et al., 2013; Berg and Brown, 1972).
evidence: Measured from high-speed tracking data and compared to literature values.

claim: MC-1 directional changes are at least one order of magnitude faster than any previously analyzed reorientation events.
source: These directional changes occur within 2.5 ms to 5 ms, at least one order of magnitude faster than any previously analyzed reorientation events (Son et al., 2013; Berg and Brown, 1972).
evidence: Comparison of measured reorientation times (2.5-5 ms) with literature values (50-100 ms).

claim: MC-1 directional changes do not occur via a continuous modulation of the ratio of radius and pitch.
source: Directional changes did not occur via a continuous modulation of the ratio of radius and pitch (Crenshaw and Edelstein-Keshet, 1993), as it has been observed as a part of the chemotaxis of sperm (Jikeli et al., 2015).
evidence: Observed from tracking data showing constant helix parameters before and after reorientation events.

claim: The helix parameters in MC-1 were the same before and after reorientation events.
source: Rather, the helix parameters were the same before and after such an event.
evidence: Measured from 3D tracking data as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: 3D tracking is essential to determine that helix parameters remain constant during reorientation, as projected 2D tracks exhibit apparent changes.
source: 3D tracking is essential to obtain this conclusion, as projected 2D tracks exhibit apparent changes in the helix parameters (see projected shadow of the track in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of 3D tracks with their 2D projections.

claim: The large helical track in MC-1 featured a pitch of ~4 µm.
source: The large helical track featured a pitch pl of ~4 µm, a radius rl of ~1 µm and a period Tl of 72 ms.
evidence: Measured from high-speed dark-field microscopy tracking at 1640 fps.

claim: The large helical track in MC-1 featured a radius of ~1 µm.
source: The large helical track featured a pitch pl of ~4 µm, a radius rl of ~1 µm and a period Tl of 72 ms.
evidence: Measured from high-speed dark-field microscopy tracking at 1640 fps.

claim: The large helical track in MC-1 featured a period of 72 ms.
source: The large helical track featured a pitch pl of ~4 µm, a radius rl of ~1 µm and a period Tl of 72 ms.
evidence: Measured from high-speed dark-field microscopy tracking at 1640 fps.

claim: The small helix in MC-1 featured a pitch of ~0.66 µm.
source: The small helix featured a pitch of ~0.66 µm, a radius rs of ~0.125 µm and a period Ts close to 14.4 ms.
evidence: Measured from high-speed dark-field microscopy tracking at 1640 fps.

claim: The small helix in MC-1 featured a radius of ~0.125 µm.
source: The small helix featured a pitch of ~0.66 µm, a radius rs of ~0.125 µm and a period Ts close to 14.4 ms.
evidence: Measured from high-speed dark-field microscopy tracking at 1640 fps.

claim: The small helix in MC-1 featured a period close to 14.4 ms.
source: The small helix featured a pitch of ~0.66 µm, a radius rs of ~0.125 µm and a period Ts close to 14.4 ms.
evidence: Measured from high-speed dark-field microscopy tracking at 1640 fps.

claim: The ratio between the large and small helix period times was close to 6 in the analyzed track.
source: The ratio between this specific track's period times was close to 6, which was later used to choose the flagella bundle's rigidities and torque in the numerical simulations.
evidence: Calculated from measured period times (72 ms / 14.4 ms ≈ 5).

claim: Each MC-1 flagella bundle features seven flagella.
source: Each bundle features seven flagella, which emerge from a cavity on the cell surface.
evidence: Observed in TEM images of MC-1 cells.

claim: MC-1 flagella bundles emerge from a cavity on the cell surface.
source: Each bundle features seven flagella, which emerge from a cavity on the cell surface.
evidence: Observed in TEM images of MC-1 cells.

claim: The individual flagella in MC-1 are bundled by a sheath.
source: The individual flagella are bundled by a sheath (scale bar is 1 µm).
evidence: Observed in TEM images of MC-1 cells.

claim: One flagella bundle position is often seen in front of the MC-1 cell relative to its swimming direction.
source: Crucially, one flagella bundle position is often seen in front of the cell (relative to its swimming direction), contrary to the model of two pushing flagella bundles, which remain behind the cell body.
evidence: Observed in high-speed dark-field microscopy tracking of flagella bundle positions.

claim: The observation of a flagella bundle in front of the cell contradicts the model of two pushing flagella bundles.
source: Crucially, one flagella bundle position is often seen in front of the cell (relative to its swimming direction), contrary to the model of two pushing flagella bundles, which remain behind the cell body.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that pushing flagella should remain behind the cell body.

claim: The bright spots' movement pattern featured the same periodicity as the large helical swimming track of the cell.
source: Additionally, the bright spots' movement pattern featured the same periodicity as the large helical swimming track of the cell (also compare Figure 3C and Figure 3D).
evidence: Observed by comparing flagella bundle position tracking with cell trajectory tracking.

claim: A motor torque of 12 pN µm was required in simulations to reproduce MC-1 movement characteristics.
source: A motor torque of 12 pN µm, about 3.5 times the motor torque of an E. coli cell, had to be chosen together with high isotropic bending and twisting rigidities of 7 pN μm2, about two times larger than for single flagella (Adhyapak and Stark, 2015).
evidence: Determined through parameter optimization in Stokesian dynamics simulations.

claim: MC-1 motor torque is about 3.5 times the motor torque of an E. coli cell.
source: A motor torque of 12 pN µm, about 3.5 times the motor torque of an E. coli cell, had to be chosen together with high isotropic bending and twisting rigidities of 7 pN μm2, about two times larger than for single flagella (Adhyapak and Stark, 2015).
evidence: Calculated from simulation parameters and comparison with known E. coli motor torque.

claim: MC-1 flagella bundles have isotropic bending and twisting rigidities of 7 pN μm2.
source: A motor torque of 12 pN µm, about 3.5 times the motor torque of an E. coli cell, had to be chosen together with high isotropic bending and twisting rigidities of 7 pN μm2, about two times larger than for single flagella (Adhyapak and Stark, 2015).
evidence: Determined through parameter optimization in Stokesian dynamics simulations.

claim: MC-1 flagella bundle rigidities are about two times larger than for single flagella.
source: A motor torque of 12 pN µm, about 3.5 times the motor torque of an E. coli cell, had to be chosen together with high isotropic bending and twisting rigidities of 7 pN μm2, about two times larger than for single flagella (Adhyapak and Stark, 2015).
evidence: Comparison with literature values for single flagella rigidities.

claim: The increased rigidity is attributed to the structure of the flagella bundle, where seven protein motors power seven sheathed flagella cooperatively.
source: We assume that this increase is attributed to the structure of the flagella bundle, where seven protein motors power seven sheathed flagella cooperatively (Figure 3A).
evidence: Inferred from TEM observations of bundle structure and simulation requirements.

claim: High torques combined with high rigidities allow for stable and high swimming velocities in MC-1.
source: Only this assumption allowed for stable and high swimming velocities in the simulations, indicating that the function of the flagella bundle is to combine high torques with high rigidities.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation results showing that only high rigidity parameters produced stable high-speed swimming.

claim: Flagella can pull cells.
source: The fact that flagella can pull cells is well established (Son et al., 2013; Constantino et al., 2016)
evidence: Cited from established literature on bacterial flagellar mechanics.

claim: Only the CCW and CW model results in the double-helical tracks experimentally observed in MC-1.
source: our simulations show that only the CCW and CW model results in the double-helical tracks experimentally observed (Figure 4A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Video 3 and Video 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by systematic comparison of different flagellar rotation scenarios in simulations.

claim: Double helical trajectories were observed for flagellar opening angles in the whole parameter range tested (30°-120°).
source: We tested the dependence of the trajectories on model parameters, in particular the opening angle and motor torque (Table 2 and Table 3). Double helical trajectories were observed for flagellar opening angles in the whole parameter range, with diameter and speed in agreement with the experiments (but no fully quantitative agreement for the pitch of the large helix).
evidence: Demonstrated through systematic parameter variation in simulations.

claim: Simulations achieved agreement with experiments for helix diameter and speed but not fully for pitch.
source: Double helical trajectories were observed for flagellar opening angles in the whole parameter range, with diameter and speed in agreement with the experiments (but no fully quantitative agreement for the pitch of the large helix).
evidence: Comparison of simulation outputs with experimental measurements.

claim: Both flagella bundles in MC-1 rotated with 100 Hz - 150 Hz in simulations.
source: Both flagella bundles rotated with 100 Hz - 150 Hz and one period of the rotation coincides with one period of the large helix in the cell's trajectory.
evidence: Measured from simulation tracking of flagella bundle positions.

claim: One period of flagella bundle rotation coincides with one period of the large helix in the cell's trajectory.
source: Both flagella bundles rotated with 100 Hz - 150 Hz and one period of the rotation coincides with one period of the large helix in the cell's trajectory. This agrees with the flagella bundle movement in the experiments (Figure 4).
evidence: Observed in both simulations and experiments through tracking of flagella bundle positions.

claim: Transiently synchronous rotations of the two flagella bundles is the most likely process for rapid reorientation in MC-1.
source: We tested different scenarios (Figure 5—figure supplements 3–5) and found a transiently synchronous rotations of the two flagella bundles to be the most likely process.
evidence: Determined by testing multiple reorientation scenarios in simulations and comparing with experimental observations.

claim: Simulated reorientation by changing from CCW/CW to CCW/CCW for 4 ms resulted in a directional change of 80° ± 8°.
source: We tested this by changing the sense of rotation from CCW and CW to CCW and CCW for 4 ms in the simulations and calculating the angle between the trajectory segments before starting and after finishing this transient CCW and CCW step (outtake in Video 5). This procedure indeed resulted in rapid reorientation with a change in direction by 80° ± 8° (Figure 4C), in agreement with the 94° ± 39° change seen in the experiments (errors are standard deviations).
evidence: Measured from simulation results of reorientation events.

claim: Experimental reorientation events showed a directional change of 94° ± 39°.
source: This procedure indeed resulted in rapid reorientation with a change in direction by 80° ± 8° (Figure 4C), in agreement with the 94° ± 39° change seen in the experiments (errors are standard deviations).
evidence: Measured from experimental tracking data of reorientation events.

claim: A transient buckling deformation was observed in the simulated flagella bundles during a reorientation event.
source: A transient buckling deformation was observed in the simulated flagella bundles during an event, which caused the fast reorientations.
evidence: Observed in simulation visualizations during reorientation events.

claim: Transient buckling deformation of flagella bundles causes fast reorientations in MC-1.
source: A transient buckling deformation was observed in the simulated flagella bundles during an event, which caused the fast reorientations.
evidence: Inferred from simulation observations showing buckling coinciding with rapid reorientation.

claim: Magnetococci are exceptional swimmers with respect to both their high speed and their reorientation swiftness.
source: Magnetococci are exceptional swimmers with respect to both their high speed and their reorientation swiftness.
evidence: Based on measured speeds over 500 µm/s and reorientation times of 2.5-5 ms, compared to other bacteria.

claim: MC-1 likely makes use of a previously unrecognized pattern of motion of their flagella bundles, with one bundle pushing the cell body and the other pulling it.
source: In addition, they are likely to make use of a previously unrecognized pattern of motion of their flagella bundles, with one bundle pushing the cell body and the other pulling it.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulations showing only CCW/CW rotation produces observed trajectories.

claim: The hierarchically organized flagella bundles provide a high torque and rigidity necessary to reach record speeds of over 200 body lengths per second.
source: The hierarchically organized flagella bundles provide a high torque and rigidity, necessary to reach record speeds of over 200 body lengths per second
evidence: Inferred from simulation requirements and TEM observations of bundle structure.

claim: The unusual type of coordination of the two bundles provides a mechanism for rapid reorientation in MC-1.
source: while the unusual type of coordination of the two bundles provides a mechanism for rapid reorientation
evidence: Demonstrated through simulations showing transient synchronous rotation produces rapid reorientation.

claim: Magnetotactic cocci such as MC-1 thrive and generally represent the most abundant MTB in aquatic environments.
source: Magnetotactic cocci such as MC-1 thrive and generally represent the most abundant MTB in aquatic environments (Lefèvre et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous ecological studies of magnetotactic bacteria.

claim: MC-1's unusual motility is an adaptation that represents a selective advantage in oxic-anoxic interfaces.
source: Their unusual motility is certainly an adaptation that represents a selective advantage that make them competitive in the highly coveted biotopes that are the oxic-anoxic interfaces (Brune et al., 2000).
evidence: Inferred from ecological context and cited literature on bacterial competition at oxic-anoxic interfaces.

claim: The swimming pattern geometry of MC-1 is reminiscent of the situation recently reported for magnetospirilla.
source: Indeed, the observed geometry of this resulting swimming pattern is reminiscent of the situation recently reported for magnetospirilla (Murat et al., 2015), despite the difference in body plan.
evidence: Comparison with cited literature on magnetospirilla swimming patterns.

claim: Magnetospirilla have two flagella at opposite cell poles and a magnetic moment parallel to the flagellar axis.
source: The magnetosprilla have two flagella at opposite cell poles, and a magnetic moment parallel to the flagellar axis, while the flagella of the cocci studied here are attached on one hemisphere of the cell and almost perpendicular to the magnetic moment.
evidence: Cited from literature on magnetospirilla morphology and compared with MC-1 observations.

claim: MC-1 flagella are attached on one hemisphere of the cell and almost perpendicular to the magnetic moment.
source: The magnetosprilla have two flagella at opposite cell poles, and a magnetic moment parallel to the flagellar axis, while the flagella of the cocci studied here are attached on one hemisphere of the cell and almost perpendicular to the magnetic moment.
evidence: Observed from TEM images and inferred from simulation results with magnetic fields.

claim: Both magnetospirilla and MC-1 swim aligned with a magnetic field with one flagellum ahead and one trailing.
source: Nevertheless, both swim aligned with a magnetic field with one flagellum ahead and one trailing.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with magnetospirilla literature and MC-1 observations.

claim: MC-1 was cultured in artificial sea water (ASW) as a base medium.
source: MC-1 was cultured similarly to the procedure reported by Bazylinski et al. (2013). Artificial sea water (ASW) was used as a base medium, containing 20 g NaCl, 6 g MgCl2, 2.4 g Na2SO4, 0.5 g KCl and 1 g CaCl2 per liter H20.
evidence: Description of experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The flagella bundle length in MC-1 was 3.3 µm ± 0.4 µm (n = 27).
source: Hence, we added the average cell radius to the mean of the flagella length. A mean flagella bundle length of 3.3 µm ± 0.4 µm (n = 27) resulted.
evidence: Measured from TEM images using ImageJ.

claim: The mean size of non-dried MC-1 cells was 1.3 µm ± 0.1 µm (n = 103).
source: The size of the non-dried cells were measured with ImageJ from images taken with a LSM780 (Zeiss; Germany) confocal microscope. The mean size was 1.3 µm ± 0.1 µm (n = 103).
evidence: Measured from confocal microscopy images using ImageJ.

claim: Each flagellum in the simulations was modeled as a helical filament discretized with 20 beads.
source: Each flagellum was modeled as a helical filament and a rotary motor. The helical filament was discretized with 20 beads with a discretization distance of 200 nm and bead diameter of 50 nm.
evidence: Description of simulation methodology.

claim: The discretization distance in the flagellum model was 200 nm.
source: The helical filament was discretized with 20 beads with a discretization distance of 200 nm and bead diameter of 50 nm.
evidence: Description of simulation methodology.

claim: The bead diameter in the flagellum model was 50 nm.
source: The helical filament was discretized with 20 beads with a discretization distance of 200 nm and bead diameter of 50 nm.
evidence: Description of simulation methodology.

claim: A stretching rigidity of 1000 pN was used in the simulations, comparable to that of single flagella.
source: Irrespective of the high motor torque and isotropic bending and twisting rigidities mentioned in the main text, a stretching rigidity of 1000 pN, comparable to that of single flagella, could be chosen.
evidence: Description of simulation parameters.

claim: A second-order Runge-Kutta algorithm was used to solve the equations of motion numerically.
source: A second-order Runge-Kutta algorithm (Sewell, 1988; Press et al., 1992) and simulation time-steps of 10−7 s were used to solve the equations of motion numerically.
evidence: Description of simulation methodology.

claim: Simulation time-steps of 10−7 s were used.
source: A second-order Runge-Kutta algorithm (Sewell, 1988; Press et al., 1992) and simulation time-steps of 10−7 s were used to solve the equations of motion numerically.
evidence: Description of simulation methodology.
